title: Cross-Text Connections, Part 1: The Method and Two Questions

beats.say: Cross-text questions give you two short texts on the same topic, called Text one and Text two. You compare their viewpoints, not just their facts.
The question usually asks how the author of Text two would respond to Text one. Sometimes it asks what both authors would agree on.

card.text: How would Text 2 respond to Text 1?

beats.say: Most often, Text one makes a claim, and Text two reacts to it. The reaction is rarely a total rejection.
Step one. Read the question first, so you know which text is responding to which.
Step two. Read Text one and write its main claim in a few words. Then read Text two the same way.
Step three. Decide how Text two relates to Text one. Does it agree, qualify, limit the scope, add a cause, or reject?
Step four. Eliminate choices whose strength does not match. Most often, a choice says reject when Text two only qualifies.
Qualifies. Text two says the claim is true but incomplete, or that it overstates things.
Limits scope. Text two says the claim is true in some settings, but may not apply to all cases.
Offers another cause. Text two says another factor may also explain the result.
Agrees and extends. Text two builds on Text one and adds to it.
Rejects. This is rare. Text two says there is no evidence, or that the claim is contradicted.
Easy question. Text one makes a claim about the benefits of street trees. Text two reports a measurement. We ask what Text two adds.

scenes.title: Text 1
scenes.text: City officials argue that planting street trees mainly benefits neighborhoods by making them more attractive to visitors.

beats.say: The claim in Text one is that street trees mainly make a neighborhood attractive to visitors.

scenes.title: Text 2
scenes.text: A team of urban researchers measured summer temperatures on streets with and without trees. Tree-lined streets were up to four degrees cooler, reducing residents' use of air conditioning.

beats.say: Text two measures something different. Tree-lined streets were cooler, and residents used less air conditioning.
So our connection is, Text two shows a cooling benefit that Text one ignores. It does not deny the attractiveness.

scenes.title: How would Text 2 respond?
scenes.question: How would the researchers in Text two most likely respond to the officials' argument in Text one?

options.A: By agreeing that attractiveness is the only benefit of street trees.
options.B: By suggesting that the argument overlooks another important benefit of street trees.
options.C: By arguing that street trees make neighborhoods less attractive.
options.D: By claiming that visitors prefer streets without trees.

beats.say: Choice A says attractiveness is the only benefit. Text two shows a second benefit, so this contradicts it.
Choice C says street trees make neighborhoods less attractive. Text two never talks about attractiveness, so there is no support.
Choice D says visitors prefer streets without trees. Text two says nothing about visitors.
Choice B adds a benefit without denying the point in Text one. That matches our connection. The answer is B.
Medium question. Now a question about what both authors would agree on. The answer must fit both texts. A claim that only one text supports is wrong.

scenes.title: Text 1
scenes.text: A town library began offering free tutoring. Within a year, the number of students visiting the library after school had doubled, and the librarians credit the tutoring program for the increase.

beats.say: Text one says that visits doubled after free tutoring began, and that the tutoring caused it.

scenes.title: Text 2
scenes.text: A second library offered free tutoring too, and its after-school visits also rose sharply. A survey there found that most of the new visitors said they came for the quiet study space, and then decided to try the tutoring.

beats.say: Text two also saw visits rise after tutoring. But the survey says the quiet study space brought many of the new visitors.

scenes.title: What would both authors agree on?
scenes.question: Based on the texts, with which statement would both authors most likely agree?

options.A: Free tutoring is the only reason students visit libraries.
options.B: Library visits by students rose after a library began offering tutoring.
options.C: Quiet study space is more valuable than tutoring.
options.D: Libraries should stop offering tutoring programs.

beats.say: Choice A says tutoring is the only reason. Text two names the quiet study space, so this does not fit both.
Choice C says the study space is more valuable. Text one never mentions it, and neither text ranks the two.
Choice D is advice. Neither text suggests that the library should stop offering its tutoring program.
Choice B is supported by both texts, because visits rose after tutoring began in each library. It does not go beyond that. The answer is B.
To recap. Read the question first, summarize each text in a few words, and name how Text two relates to Text one.
For a both-agree question, the answer must fit both texts. In the next video, we work through a hard question and the common traps.
